items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "mitochondrion"?
options: Contains the genetic material (chromosomes made of DNA) that controls the activities of the cell.
Site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy for the cell.
A small extra ring of DNA in a bacterial cell, carrying a few genes.
items.answer: Site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy for the cell.
items.markingKey: Mitochondrion: site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy for the cell.

items.stem: Root hair cells are plant cells but they have no chloroplasts. Explain why.
items.answer: They are underground, so they receive no light and cannot photosynthesise; chloroplasts would be of no use.
items.markingKey: no light reaches roots [1]; chloroplasts only needed for photosynthesis [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a plant cell placed in water does not burst, but an animal cell may.
items.answer: The plant cell wall is strong and resists further expansion as the cell becomes turgid; animal cells have only a cell membrane, which bursts.
items.markingKey: cell wall resists expansion [1]; animal cell has no wall [1] [2]

items.stem: A cell is examined under a microscope. Structures seen: cell wall, circular DNA, ribosome. Structures not present: nucleus, chloroplast. What type of cell is it?
items.answer: A bacterial cell
items.markingKey: Present cell wall, circular DNA, ribosome and absent nucleus, chloroplast → bacterial cell.

items.stem: A cell is examined under a microscope. Structures seen: ribosome, mitochondrion, cell membrane, cytoplasm. Structures not present: cell wall, plasmid. (a) Identify the type of cell and give a reason. (b) State the function of the cell membrane. (c) Suggest which of these samples it came from: a cell from a moss leaf, a palisade cell from a leaf, cheek cells from the lining of the mouth.
items.answer: (a) animal cell: it has a mitochondrion but no cell wall. (b) Controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell (partially permeable). (c) cheek cells from the lining of the mouth
items.markingKey: (a) animal [1] with reason from structures [1] (b) controls the movement of substances into and out of the cell (partially permeable) [1] (c) cheek cells from the lining of the mouth [1] [4]

items.stem: A cell is examined under a microscope. Structures seen: cytoplasm, cell wall, chloroplast, large permanent vacuole. Structures not present: circular DNA, plasmid. (a) Identify the type of cell and give a reason. (b) State the function of the cell wall. (c) Suggest which of these samples it came from: cells from a liver sample, a cell from a culture of soil bacteria, a cell from the epidermis of an onion bulb.
items.answer: (a) plant cell: it has a large permanent vacuole and a nucleus. (b) Surrounds the cell membrane; strengthens and supports the cell and stops it bursting. (c) a cell from the epidermis of an onion bulb
items.markingKey: (a) plant [1] with reason from structures [1] (b) surrounds the cell membrane; strengthens and supports the cell and stops it bursting [1] (c) a cell from the epidermis of an onion bulb [1] [4]

items.stem: Diego prepares a slide of rhubarb epidermis using water only and observes it with a light microscope in a school laboratory in Lisbon. (a) State two rules for making a biological drawing of the cells. (b) Explain why ribosomes cannot be seen in these cells with this microscope.
items.answer: (a) Use a sharp pencil with clear continuous lines, no shading; draw large, label with ruled lines, include a title and magnification. (b) Ribosomes are too small; the light microscope does not have a high enough resolution (an electron microscope is needed).
items.markingKey: (a) any two rules [2] (b) too small [1]; need electron microscope / higher resolution [1] [2]

items.stem: Hana prepares a slide of a moss leaf using water only and observes it with a light microscope in a school laboratory in Cairo. (a) Name three structures that should be visible in these cells with a light microscope. (b) Explain why ribosomes cannot be seen in these cells with this microscope.
items.answer: (a) nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm. (b) Ribosomes are too small; the light microscope does not have a high enough resolution (an electron microscope is needed).
items.markingKey: (a) any three from: nucleus, cell membrane, cytoplasm, cell wall, large permanent vacuole, chloroplast [3] (b) too small [1]; need electron microscope / higher resolution [1] [2]

items.stem: Which structures are found in both plant cells and bacterial cells?
options: Cell wall, cell membrane and ribosomes
items.answer: Cell wall, cell membrane and ribosomes
items.markingKey: Bacteria and plants both have walls (different materials), membranes, cytoplasm and ribosomes; bacteria lack a nucleus, mitochondria and chloroplasts.

items.stem: Explain why cells that need a lot of energy, such as muscle cells, contain many mitochondria.
items.answer: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which releases energy; more mitochondria allow more respiration and more energy release.
items.markingKey: mitochondria = aerobic respiration [1]; more energy released for contraction [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how you would prepare a slide of onion epidermis cells to view with a light microscope.
items.answer: Peel a thin layer of epidermis, place it flat in a drop of water or iodine on a slide, lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles, then view on low power first.
items.markingKey: thin layer [1]; stain (iodine) [1]; coverslip lowered at angle [1] [3]

items.stem: State the function of each cell structure: (i) cytoplasm (ii) plasmid (iii) circular DNA.
items.answer: (i) jelly-like fluid where most of the chemical reactions of the cell take place (ii) a small extra ring of DNA in a bacterial cell, carrying a few genes (iii) a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm that carries the genes of a bacterium
items.markingKey: (i) jelly-like fluid where most of the chemical reactions of the cell take place [1]; (ii) a small extra ring of DNA in a bacterial cell, carrying a few genes [1]; (iii) a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm that carries the genes of a bacterium [1] [3]

items.stem: State the function of each cell structure: (i) chloroplast (ii) plasmid (iii) large permanent vacuole. For each one, name a type of cell (animal, plant or bacterial) in which it is found.
items.answer: (i) contains chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis (plant) (ii) a small extra ring of DNA in a bacterial cell, carrying a few genes (bacterial) (iii) contains cell sap; keeps the cell turgid and stores dissolved substances (plant)
items.markingKey: (i) contains chlorophyll, which absorbs light energy for photosynthesis [1]; (ii) a small extra ring of DNA in a bacterial cell, carrying a few genes [1]; (iii) contains cell sap; keeps the cell turgid and stores dissolved substances [1] ; one correct cell type each [1] [4]

items.stem: A cell is examined under a microscope. Structures seen: cytoplasm, circular DNA, cell membrane, ribosome. Structures not present: nucleus, chloroplast. (a) Identify the type of cell and give a reason. (b) State the function of the circular DNA. (c) Suggest which of these samples it came from: a cell from a moss leaf, a palisade cell from a leaf, a cell from a sample of yoghurt.
items.answer: (a) bacterial cell: it has circular DNA and no nucleus. (b) A single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm that carries the genes of a bacterium. (c) a cell from a sample of yoghurt
items.markingKey: (a) bacterial [1] with reason from structures [1] (b) a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm that carries the genes of a bacterium [1] (c) a cell from a sample of yoghurt [1] [4]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "organ system"?
options: A cell whose structure is adapted to carry out a particular function.
A living thing made of one or more organ systems working together.
A group of organs with related functions, working together to perform body functions.
A group of cells with similar structures, working together to perform a shared function.
items.answer: A group of organs with related functions, working together to perform body functions.
items.markingKey: Organ system: a group of organs with related functions, working together to perform body functions.

items.stem: Explain how the structure of a red blood cell is adapted to its function.
items.answer: No nucleus leaves more room for haemoglobin; biconcave shape gives a large surface area for oxygen diffusion; small and flexible to squeeze through capillaries.
items.markingKey: two features linked to function [2] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a sperm cell contains many mitochondria.
items.answer: Mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, releasing energy for the flagellum to swim to the egg.
items.markingKey: respiration releases energy [1]; for swimming / flagellum movement [1] [2]

items.stem: A cell has a large cytoplasm containing energy stores (jelly coat). Its function is that it is fertilised and provides nutrients for the early embryo. Which cell is it?
items.answer: Egg cell
items.markingKey: Egg cell: a large cytoplasm containing energy stores (jelly coat) — adaptation for: is fertilised and provides nutrients for the early embryo.

items.stem: Specialised cells have features related to their functions. (a) Name the cell that moves mucus, which traps dust and pathogens, up the trachea and bronchi and describe one adaptation it has. (b) Describe how one feature of a root hair cell is related to its function.
items.answer: (a) ciliated cell: cilia (tiny hairs) on its surface. (b) A long extension that increases the surface area, so it absorbs water and mineral ions from the soil.
items.markingKey: (a) ciliated cell [1]; adaptation: cilia (tiny hairs) on its surface [1] (b) feature [1] linked to function: absorbs water and mineral ions from the soil [1] [4]

items.stem: Noah is studying a ciliated cell using a microscope and an electron micrograph. The cell moves mucus, which traps dust and pathogens, up the trachea and bronchi. (a) Describe one structural feature of the ciliated cell that adapts it to this function. (b) Explain why multicellular organisms need specialised cells, while single-celled organisms do not.
items.answer: (a) Cilia (tiny hairs) on its surface. (b) In large organisms most cells are far from the surface and many functions are needed; division of labour lets cells become efficient at one job. A single cell must carry out all processes itself.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] feature; [1] linked to function [2] (b) division of labour / efficiency [1]; large organisms need different functions in different places [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain how a root hair cell is adapted for absorbing water.
items.answer: The long hair-like extension gives a large surface area for osmosis and active uptake of ions; thin wall; no chloroplasts needed.
items.markingKey: large surface area [1]; linked to faster uptake [1] [2]

items.stem: State whether each is a cell, a tissue, an organ or an organ system. (i) palisade mesophyll (ii) a shoot system (iii) the kidney (iv) a neurone.
items.answer: (i) tissue (ii) organ system (iii) organ (iv) cell
items.markingKey: (i) tissue; (ii) organ system; (iii) organ; (iv) cell (four correct [3]; three [2]; two [1]) [3]

items.stem: State whether each is a cell, a tissue, an organ or an organ system. (i) a root (ii) the digestive system (iii) a guard cell (iv) palisade mesophyll.
items.answer: (i) organ (ii) organ system (iii) cell (iv) tissue
items.markingKey: (i) organ; (ii) organ system; (iii) cell; (iv) tissue (four correct [3]; three [2]; two [1]) [3]

items.stem: Kwame is studying a red blood cell using a microscope and an electron micrograph. The cell transports oxygen. (a) Describe one structural feature of the red blood cell that adapts it to this function. (b) Suggest what would happen to the function of the red blood cell if this feature were missing. (c) Explain why multicellular organisms need specialised cells, while single-celled organisms do not.
items.answer: (a) No nucleus, a biconcave shape and haemoglobin. (b) It would be less able to carry out its function (transports oxygen) efficiently. (c) In large organisms most cells are far from the surface and many functions are needed; division of labour lets cells become efficient at one job. A single cell must carry out all processes itself.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] feature; [1] linked to function [2] (b) reduced efficiency linked to feature [2] (c) division of labour / efficiency [1]; large organisms need different functions in different places [1] [2]

items.stem: Convert 1.5 mm into micrometres (μm).
A student calculates that a cheek cell 8 mm long in a drawing at ×160 has an actual size of 0.05 μm. Explain the error and give the correct answer.
items.answer: They divided correctly (8 ÷ 160 = 0.05) but the answer is in mm, not μm; 0.05 mm = 50 μm.
items.markingKey: answer is in mm [1]; correct value 50 μm [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why a scale bar is often more useful than a stated magnification on a printed micrograph.
items.answer: If the image is enlarged or reduced when printed or on screen, the scale bar changes size with the image, so it still gives the correct scale; a stated magnification would then be wrong.
items.markingKey: image size may change [1]; scale bar changes with it [1] [2]

items.stem: A drawing of a palisade cell has a length of 36 mm. The magnification of the drawing is ×500. Calculate the actual length of a palisade cell in micrometres (μm).
items.markingKey: actual size = image size ÷ magnification [1]; 36 ÷ 500 = 0.0720 mm [1]; × 1000 = 72.0 μm [1] [3]

items.stem: A drawing of a red blood cell has a length of 12 mm. The magnification of the drawing is ×2000. Calculate the actual length of a red blood cell in micrometres (μm).
items.markingKey: actual size = image size ÷ magnification [1]; 12 ÷ 2000 = 0.00600 mm [1]; × 1000 = 6.00 μm [1] [3]

items.stem: A drawing of a cheek cell has a length of 32 mm. The magnification of the drawing is ×500. Calculate the actual length of a cheek cell in micrometres (μm). Show your working.
items.markingKey: actual size = image size ÷ magnification [1]; 32 ÷ 500 = 0.0640 mm [1]; × 1000 = 64.0 μm [1] [3]

items.stem: Freya makes a drawing of a red blood cell from a microscope slide. The drawing is 10.3 mm long and the actual length is 6.87 μm. A textbook micrograph of a palisade cell is 23 mm long at ×500. (a) Calculate how many times longer the larger specimen is than the smaller one. (b) Suggest why measuring several specimens and calculating a mean gives a better estimate of actual size.
items.answer: (a) 6.70 times (b) Individual cells vary in size and measurements have errors; a mean of several reduces the effect of unusual cells and random error.
items.markingKey: (a) 46.0 ÷ 6.87 = 6.70 [2] (b) variation between specimens [1]; mean reduces effect of random error [1] [2]

items.stem: Priya makes a drawing of a stoma (guard cell pair) from a microscope slide. The drawing is 40 mm long and the actual length is 40.0 μm. A textbook micrograph of an ant head is 76 mm long at ×40. (a) Calculate the magnification of the drawing. (b) Suggest why measuring several specimens and calculating a mean gives a better estimate of actual size. (c) State one rule for drawing biological specimens accurately.
items.answer: (a) ×1000 (b) Individual cells vary in size and measurements have errors; a mean of several reduces the effect of unusual cells and random error. (c) Draw proportions accurately with clear continuous pencil lines and no shading.
items.markingKey: (a) convert 40 mm to 40000 μm [1]; ÷ 40.0 = ×1000 [1] [2] (b) variation between specimens [1]; mean reduces effect of random error [1] [2] (c) [1]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "resolution"?
options: The ability to distinguish two points that are close together as separate.
An image produced using an electron microscope, showing more detail than a light microscope.
How many times larger an image is than the real object (image size ÷ actual size).
One thousandth of a millimetre (1 μm = 0.001 mm).
items.answer: The ability to distinguish two points that are close together as separate.
items.markingKey: Resolution: the ability to distinguish two points that are close together as separate.

items.stem: Explain why ribosomes can be seen in electron micrographs but not with a light microscope.
items.answer: Electron microscopes have a much higher resolution (and magnification), so very small structures such as ribosomes can be distinguished.
items.markingKey: higher resolution [1]; ribosomes too small for light microscope [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe how you would estimate the actual width of a cell using a light microscope and a ruler or eyepiece graticule.
items.answer: Calibrate the graticule with a stage micrometer (or measure the field of view), count the divisions across the cell, convert divisions to μm using the calibration, repeat for several cells and find the mean.
items.markingKey: calibrate [1]; measure divisions [1]; convert and average several cells [1] [3]

items.stem: Sofia photographs a bacterium through a microscope. The image is 14 mm long and the actual length is 1.40 μm. Calculate the magnification of the image.
items.markingKey: magnification = image size ÷ actual size [1]; convert to same units: 14 mm = 14000 μm [1]; 14000 ÷ 1.40 = ×10000 [1] [3]

items.stem: Describe how to calculate the actual size of a cell from a micrograph that has a scale bar.
items.answer: Measure the scale bar in mm and convert to μm; magnification = measured bar length ÷ value written on the bar; measure the image of the cell; actual size = image size ÷ magnification; keep units consistent.
items.markingKey: measure bar [1]; magnification from bar [1]; measure cell image [1]; actual = image ÷ M [1]; units consistent [1] [5]

items.stem: Isla makes a drawing of a flea from a microscope slide. The drawing is 96 mm long and the actual length is 2400 μm. A textbook micrograph of a paramecium is 94 mm long at ×400. (a) Calculate the magnification of the drawing. (b) Calculate the actual length of a paramecium in μm. (c) State one rule for drawing biological specimens accurately.
items.answer: (a) ×40.0 (b) 235 μm (c) Draw proportions accurately with clear continuous pencil lines and no shading.

items.stem: Which term is defined as "an organelle where aerobic respiration takes place"?
items.answer: Mitochondrion
items.markingKey: Mitochondrion: an organelle where aerobic respiration takes place.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "cell division"?
options: A small membrane-bound sac that transports substances within a cell.
A very small structure where proteins are made.
A network of membranes covered with ribosomes, where proteins are made and transported.
The process by which an existing cell divides to produce new cells.
items.answer: The process by which an existing cell divides to produce new cells.
items.markingKey: Cell division: the process by which an existing cell divides to produce new cells.

items.stem: Cells in the pancreas make and secrete large amounts of enzymes. Explain why they contain a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and many vesicles.
items.answer: Enzymes are proteins made on ribosomes on the RER; vesicles carry the enzymes to the cell membrane for secretion.
items.markingKey: RER / ribosomes make protein [1]; vesicles transport for secretion [1] [2]

items.stem: A cell in a culture divides every 20 minutes. Starting with one cell, how many cells will there be after 60 minutes?
items.answer: 8 cells
items.markingKey: number of divisions = 60 ÷ 20 = 3 [1]; 1 × 2^3 = 8 [1] [2]

items.stem: An electron micrograph shows a cell from the salivary gland that secretes amylase. It contains a large nucleus, many mitochondria, a lot of rough endoplasmic reticulum and many vesicles near the cell membrane. (a) Suggest why there are many vesicles near the cell membrane. (b) State how the cell would have been produced.
items.answer: (a) The vesicles carry the proteins made by the cell to the membrane for release (protein (enzyme) secretion). (b) By division of an existing cell (mitosis).
items.markingKey: (a) transport [1]; release/secretion of proteins at the membrane [1] [2] (b) [1]

items.stem: Explain why a growing root tip contains many cells dividing, but a mature leaf contains few.
items.answer: Growth needs new cells, which are produced only by division of existing cells; mature tissue has stopped growing so few cells divide.
items.markingKey: new cells only from division [1]; growth regions need new cells [1] [2]

items.stem: A yeast cell divides every 60 minutes. Starting with one cell, how many cells will there be after 6 hours?
items.answer: 64 cells

items.stem: Which structure is present in a cheek cell but absent from a bacterial cell?
items.answer: Nucleus
items.markingKey: Bacteria are prokaryotes: no nucleus or mitochondria.

items.stem: Explain why iodine solution is added to onion cells before viewing them.
items.answer: It stains the nucleus and cytoplasm (and starch) so that the cell structures can be seen more clearly; the cells are almost colourless otherwise.
items.markingKey: stain gives contrast [1]; makes nucleus / cell parts visible [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the cell membrane is described as partially permeable.
items.answer: It lets some substances (such as water, oxygen and glucose) pass through but stops others, such as large molecules, so it controls what enters and leaves the cell.
items.markingKey: some substances pass, others do not [1]; controls entry and exit [1] [2]

items.stem: A cell is examined under a microscope. Structures seen: large permanent vacuole, chloroplast, mitochondrion. Structures not present: circular DNA, plasmid. What type of cell is it?
items.answer: A plant cell
items.markingKey: Present large permanent vacuole, chloroplast, mitochondrion and absent circular DNA, plasmid → plant cell.

items.stem: State the function of each cell structure: (i) cell wall (ii) cytoplasm (iii) ribosome.
items.answer: (i) surrounds the cell membrane; strengthens and supports the cell and stops it bursting (ii) jelly-like fluid where most of the chemical reactions of the cell take place (iii) site of protein synthesis
items.markingKey: (i) surrounds the cell membrane; strengthens and supports the cell and stops it bursting [1]; (ii) jelly-like fluid where most of the chemical reactions of the cell take place [1]; (iii) site of protein synthesis [1] [3]

items.stem: Compare the structure of a palisade mesophyll cell with the structure of a bacterial cell.
items.answer: Both: cell wall (cellulose in palisade, not cellulose in bacteria), cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes. Palisade: nucleus, chloroplasts, mitochondria, large vacuole. Bacterium: no nucleus, circular DNA and plasmids, no chloroplasts or mitochondria, much smaller.
items.markingKey: two similarities [2]; three differences [3] [5]

items.stem: Which list shows the levels of organisation in the correct order, from smallest to largest?
items.answer: cell → tissue → organ → organ system
items.markingKey: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form organ systems.

items.stem: Explain why the stomach is described as an organ.
items.answer: It is made of several different tissues (muscle, glandular epithelium, connective tissue) working together to perform a function (digestion).
items.markingKey: several tissues [1]; working together for a function [1] [2]

items.stem: A cell has many chloroplasts near the upper surface of the leaf. Its function is that it carries out photosynthesis. Which cell is it?
items.answer: Palisade mesophyll cell
items.markingKey: Palisade mesophyll cell: many chloroplasts near the upper surface of the leaf — adaptation for: carries out photosynthesis.

items.stem: Using named examples, explain the differences between a cell, a tissue, an organ and an organ system.
items.answer: Cell: basic unit, e.g. muscle cell. Tissue: group of similar cells with a shared function, e.g. muscle tissue. Organ: several tissues working together, e.g. heart. Organ system: organs with related functions, e.g. circulatory system.
items.markingKey: each level defined with example [4] [4]

items.stem: Describe how the structures of a ciliated cell, a red blood cell and a sperm cell are adapted to their functions.
items.answer: Ciliated: cilia beat to move mucus. RBC: no nucleus, biconcave, haemoglobin for oxygen transport. Sperm: flagellum to swim, mitochondria for energy, acrosome enzymes to digest egg coat.
items.markingKey: one adaptation linked to function for each cell [3]; extra detail [2] [5]

items.stem: Convert 0.008 mm into micrometres (μm).
items.answer: 8 μm

items.stem: A student in Nairobi states: "Magnification should be given in mm because the image was measured in mm." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Magnification is a ratio with no units, written as ×number.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Magnification is a ratio with no units, written as ×number. [2]

items.stem: Tariq says: "1 mm is equal to 100 μm." Explain whether Tariq is correct.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: 1 mm = 1000 μm. [2]

items.stem: A micrograph of an ant head has a scale bar labelled 200 μm. The scale bar measures 8 mm on the page and the image of an ant head measures 32 mm. (a) Calculate the magnification of the micrograph. (b) Calculate the actual length of an ant head.
Leila photographs an ant head through a microscope. The image is 64 mm long and the actual length is 1600 μm. Calculate the magnification of the image. State the formula you use.
items.markingKey: magnification = image size ÷ actual size [1]; convert to same units: 64 mm = 64000 μm [1]; 64000 ÷ 1600 = ×40 [1] [3]

items.stem: Samuel makes a drawing of an amoeba from a microscope slide. The drawing is 48 mm long and the actual length is 480 μm. A textbook micrograph of a paramecium is 61 mm long at ×400. (a) Calculate the magnification of the drawing. (b) Calculate the actual length of a paramecium in μm. (c) State one rule for drawing biological specimens accurately.
items.answer: (a) ×100 (b) 152 μm (c) Draw proportions accurately with clear continuous pencil lines and no shading.

items.stem: Explain why the number of mitochondria differs between different types of cell.
items.answer: Cells that need more energy (muscle, sperm, root hair cells taking up ions) carry out more aerobic respiration, so they have more mitochondria.
items.markingKey: mitochondria = respiration / energy [1]; linked to energy demand [1] [2]

items.stem: A scientist counted the mean number of mitochondria per cell in electron micrographs of three cell types: skin surface cell: 164; root hair cell: 343; liver cell: 1918. (a) Identify the cell type with the most mitochondria. (b) Explain why this cell type needs many mitochondria.
items.answer: (a) liver cell (b) It needs a lot of energy (e.g. for contraction / active processes); mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, which releases energy.
items.markingKey: (a) liver cell [1] (b) high energy demand [1]; mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration [1] [3]

items.stem: A scientist counted the mean number of mitochondria per cell in electron micrographs of three cell types: neurone: 1314; root hair cell: 525; skin surface cell: 198. (a) Identify the cell type with the most mitochondria. (b) Explain why this cell type needs many mitochondria. (c) Calculate how many times more mitochondria the neurone has than the skin surface cell.
items.answer: (a) neurone (b) It needs a lot of energy (e.g. for contraction / active processes); mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, which releases energy. (c) 6.64 times
items.markingKey: (a) neurone [1] (b) high energy demand [1]; mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration [1] (c) 1314 ÷ 198 = 6.64 [1] [4]

items.stem: A cell has a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole. What type of cell is it?
items.answer: A plant cell
items.markingKey: Chloroplasts and a permanent vacuole are found only in plant cells (of these types).

items.stem: Aisha says: "Animal cells do not have mitochondria because only plant cells respire." Explain whether Aisha is correct.
items.answer: Animal and plant cells both contain mitochondria and respire aerobically.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Animal and plant cells both contain mitochondria and respire aerobically. [2]

items.stem: A student in Singapore states: "All plant cells contain chloroplasts." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Only cells that receive light, such as palisade and spongy mesophyll cells, contain chloroplasts; root cells do not.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Only cells that receive light, such as palisade and spongy mesophyll cells, contain chloroplasts; root cells do not. [2]

items.stem: A cell is examined under a microscope. Structures seen: chloroplast, large permanent vacuole, nucleus. Structures not present: circular DNA, plasmid. What type of cell is it?
items.answer: A plant cell
items.markingKey: Present chloroplast, large permanent vacuole, nucleus and absent circular DNA, plasmid → plant cell.

items.stem: State the function of each cell structure: (i) cytoplasm (ii) circular DNA (iii) cell wall.
items.answer: (i) jelly-like fluid where most of the chemical reactions of the cell take place (ii) a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm that carries the genes of a bacterium (iii) surrounds the cell membrane; strengthens and supports the cell and stops it bursting
items.markingKey: (i) jelly-like fluid where most of the chemical reactions of the cell take place [1]; (ii) a single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm that carries the genes of a bacterium [1]; (iii) surrounds the cell membrane; strengthens and supports the cell and stops it bursting [1] [3]

items.stem: Lina prepares a slide of a moss leaf using water only and observes it with a light microscope in a school laboratory in Kathmandu. (a) Describe how the slide should be prepared. (b) State two rules for making a biological drawing of the cells.
items.answer: (a) Thin layer of cells on slide, drop of stain/water, coverslip lowered at an angle to avoid air bubbles, blot excess. (b) Use a sharp pencil with clear continuous lines, no shading; draw large, label with ruled lines, include a title and magnification.
items.markingKey: (a) thin layer / single layer of cells [1]; add stain [1]; coverslip at angle to avoid bubbles [1] [3] (b) any two rules [2]

items.stem: Which cell has a biconcave shape and no nucleus?
items.answer: Red blood cell
items.markingKey: More room for haemoglobin, larger surface area for diffusion of oxygen.

items.stem: Explain the role of ciliated cells in protecting the lungs.
items.answer: Cilia beat to sweep mucus, which has trapped dust and pathogens, up and out of the airways so they do not reach the alveoli.
items.markingKey: cilia move mucus [1]; removes trapped pathogens / dust [1] [2]

items.stem: A cell has no nucleus, a biconcave shape and haemoglobin. Its function is that it transports oxygen. Which cell is it?
items.answer: Red blood cell
items.markingKey: Red blood cell: no nucleus, a biconcave shape and haemoglobin — adaptation for: transports oxygen.

items.stem: Leila is studying a red blood cell using a microscope and an electron micrograph. The cell transports oxygen. (a) Describe one structural feature of the red blood cell that adapts it to this function. (b) Name the next level of organisation formed when many of these cells work together, and give an example.
items.answer: (a) No nucleus, a biconcave shape and haemoglobin. (b) A tissue, e.g. blood.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] feature; [1] linked to function [2] (b) tissue [1]; example [1] [2]

items.stem: Samuel is studying a root hair cell using a microscope and an electron micrograph. The cell absorbs water and mineral ions from the soil. (a) Name the next level of organisation formed when many of these cells work together, and give an example. (b) Explain why multicellular organisms need specialised cells, while single-celled organisms do not.
items.answer: (a) A tissue, e.g. root epidermis. (b) In large organisms most cells are far from the surface and many functions are needed; division of labour lets cells become efficient at one job. A single cell must carry out all processes itself.
items.markingKey: (a) tissue [1]; example [1] [2] (b) division of labour / efficiency [1]; large organisms need different functions in different places [1] [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "magnification"?
options: A line on a micrograph labelled with the actual length it represents.
One thousandth of a millimetre (1 μm = 0.001 mm).
The ability to distinguish two points that are close together as separate.
How many times larger an image is than the real object (image size ÷ actual size).
items.answer: How many times larger an image is than the real object (image size ÷ actual size).
items.markingKey: Magnification: how many times larger an image is than the real object (image size ÷ actual size).

items.stem: A student in Lisbon states: "To find the actual size you multiply the image size by the magnification." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification. [2]

items.stem: Nadia writes in a revision note: "To find the actual size you multiply the image size by the magnification." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Actual size = image size ÷ magnification. [2]

items.stem: A micrograph of an amoeba has a scale bar labelled 1000 μm. The scale bar measures 40 mm on the page and the image of an amoeba measures 12.6 mm. (a) Calculate the magnification of the micrograph. (b) Calculate the actual length of an amoeba.
A drawing of a flea has a length of 115 mm. The magnification of the drawing is ×50. Calculate the actual length of a flea in micrometres (μm).
items.markingKey: actual size = image size ÷ magnification [1]; 115 ÷ 50 = 2.30 mm [1]; × 1000 = 2300 μm [1] [3]

items.stem: Daniel makes a drawing of an onion epidermal cell from a microscope slide. The drawing is 147 mm long and the actual length is 294 μm. A textbook micrograph of a mitochondrion is 18 mm long at ×10000. (a) Calculate the magnification of the drawing. (b) Calculate the actual length of a mitochondrion in μm. (c) State one rule for drawing biological specimens accurately.
items.answer: (a) ×500 (b) 1.80 μm (c) Draw proportions accurately with clear continuous pencil lines and no shading.

items.stem: Explain why bacteria contain ribosomes but no mitochondria.
items.answer: All cells must make proteins, so they need ribosomes; bacteria are prokaryotes with no membrane-bound organelles, and respire using enzymes in the cytoplasm and membrane.
items.markingKey: all cells make proteins [1]; prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles [1] [2]

items.stem: A scientist counted the mean number of mitochondria per cell in electron micrographs of three cell types: root hair cell: 338; heart muscle cell: 5477; neurone: 963. (a) Identify the cell type with the most mitochondria. (b) Explain why this cell type needs many mitochondria.
items.answer: (a) heart muscle cell (b) It needs a lot of energy (e.g. for contraction / active processes); mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, which releases energy.
items.markingKey: (a) heart muscle cell [1] (b) high energy demand [1]; mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration [1] [3]

items.stem: A scientist counted the mean number of mitochondria per cell in electron micrographs of three cell types: neurone: 899; fat storage cell: 235; skin surface cell: 159. (a) Identify the cell type with the most mitochondria. (b) Explain why this cell type needs many mitochondria. (c) Calculate how many times more mitochondria the neurone has than the skin surface cell.
items.answer: (a) neurone (b) It needs a lot of energy (e.g. for contraction / active processes); mitochondria carry out aerobic respiration, which releases energy. (c) 5.65 times
items.markingKey: (a) neurone [1] (b) high energy demand [1]; mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration [1] (c) 899 ÷ 159 = 5.65 [1] [4]
